pedagogy.summary: At KS3 (ages 11-13) children construct and interpret the full family of statistical displays — frequency tables (including GROUPED tables for continuous/large numerical data), bar charts, pie charts, pictograms and vertical line charts — for both categorical and grouped numerical data, and crucially CHOOSE the representation that fits the data type. Two ideas do the teaching work. First, grouping continuous data into class intervals demands intervals that are equal, non-overlapping and gap-free, so every value falls in exactly one class — which is why inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) matters, to fix where a boundary value goes. Second, the representation must match the data: categorical data suits bar charts and pie charts; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histograms; only genuinely continuous time-series data suits a line graph. The characteristic errors are ambiguous or overlapping class boundaries, and reaching for the wrong chart for the data type (e.g. a line graph joining categories, or a pie chart where the 'whole' is meaningless). Because this is representational, understanding shows in CONSTRUCTING a display, not just reading one.
bestPractices: Group continuous data into equal, non-overlapping, gap-free class intervals that cover the whole range, using inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20…) so each value — especially a boundary value — belongs to exactly one class
Use tally marks when counting raw data into a frequency table to avoid miscounts

Teach the representation as a CHOICE driven by data type: categorical → bar chart or pie chart; grouped continuous → touching bars/histogram; proportions of a whole → pie chart; genuine time-series → line graph
Contrast a bar chart (categorical, bars with gaps) with a histogram-style display (continuous, bars touching) so children see why the data type changes the display
Compute pie-chart sector angles as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and check they sum to 360°
Interpret comparative charts by drawing a CONCLUSION about the difference between data sets, not just reading a single value
keyRepresentations: A grouped frequency table with class intervals in inequality notation and a tally column
A bar chart (categorical, gaps between bars) set beside a histogram-style display (continuous, bars touching) for the same kind of contrast
A pie chart with sectors as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°
A 'which chart?' decision aid keyed to data type (categorical / grouped continuous / proportion / time-series)
commonMisconceptions: Choosing overlapping or ambiguous class intervals (0-10, 10-20) so a boundary value could go in either class, or leaving gaps that omit values
Choosing a representation that doesn't fit the data type — e.g. a line graph joining categorical bars, or a pie chart where the whole is not meaningful
Calculating pie-chart angles by dividing 360° by the frequency instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total
Miscounting raw data into the table (helped by tallying), or reading a single value from a comparative chart instead of concluding about the difference

learn.summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) construct and interpret the full family of statistical displays — frequency tables (including GROUPED tables for continuous/large numerical data), bar charts, pie charts, pictograms and vertical line charts — and crucially CHOOSE the representation that fits the data type. Two ideas do the teaching work. First, grouping continuous data demands class intervals that are non-overlapping and gap-free, so every value falls in exactly one class — which is why inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) matters, to fix where a boundary value goes; equal class widths are the usual KS3 choice so that bar heights can be compared fairly, but equal widths are not what puts each value in exactly one class. Second, the representation must match the data: categorical data suits bar charts, pie charts or pictograms; ungrouped discrete numerical data suits a vertical line chart; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histograms; proportions of a whole suit a pie chart; genuine time-series data suits a line graph. Because this skill is representational, understanding shows in CONSTRUCTING a display, not just reading one.

activities.title: Grouped-table-and-chart workshop (set intervals, then choose a chart)
feedback: If two intervals share an endpoint without inequality notation (e.g. 0-10 and 10-20), ask where exactly 10 goes; switch to 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20 so it settles into one class.
If any value falls in no class, your intervals have a gap — extend or adjust them so they cover the whole range without gaps.

If you join categorical bars with a line, point out the line implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histogram (or a frequency polygon plotted at class midpoints), and categorical data suits a bar chart with gaps.
For a pie chart, if the sectors do not sum to 360°, recheck each angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° rather than 360° ÷ frequency.
activities.rationale: Constructing a table and choosing/building a chart makes the interval and representation decisions consequential rather than abstract, which is where the two discriminating judgements become visible. A live builder where boundary values flag until the notation is unambiguous, and a 'choose the chart' surface that draws the mismatched choice, are optional mechanisms that may make the learning concrete; equivalent work can be done on paper with teacher feedback.
sourceClaims: Numerical data can be organised into grouped data with class intervals; class intervals can be written in different ways and care is needed with the inequalities so an item (especially a boundary/minimum/maximum value) goes into the correct group; tally marks help avoid miscounts when filling in frequencies

Representations should be chosen to fit the data type: categorical data is displayed with bar graphs/pie charts, while numerical (measurement) data uses displays with a measurement scale; distinguishing categorical from numerical data is foundational to choosing a display
Pie chart sector angles are (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and must sum to 360°; a named misconception is dividing 360° by the frequency

KS3 pupils construct and interpret appropriate tables, charts and diagrams, including frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data
learnerActions: Take a strip of raw running times (e.g. 30 runners' times to the nearest second) and set your own class-interval boundaries so the intervals are equal, non-overlapping and gap-free and cover the whole range.
Place each raw value into exactly one class; deliberately try writing intervals as 0-10 and 10-20, then find where a runner who took exactly 10 seconds goes — notice the ambiguity.
Rewrite the intervals using inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20…) and confirm the boundary value now has exactly one home.
Choose which chart suits this data — bar chart, pie chart, line graph or histogram-style touching bars — then draw it and check the drawing against the data type.
If you choose a pie chart, compute each sector angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and check the angles sum to 360°.
activities.intendedInsight: Boundary ambiguity is resolved by inequality notation so every value belongs to exactly one class; and the chart must match the data type — a line joining categorical bars implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist, whereas grouped continuous data is shown with touching bars (a frequency polygon through class midpoints is a separate, legitimate display for grouped continuous data).

activities.title: Count raw data into a frequency table with tallies
feedback: If your frequencies do not sum to the number of data items, recount the tallies for the disputed rows.
If a value seems to belong to two class rows, your intervals overlap — fix them with inequality notation so each value lands in exactly one class.
activities.rationale: Accurate counting into a table is a prerequisite for every downstream display; tally marks are the standard technique to avoid miscounts.
sourceClaims: Numerical data can be organised into grouped data with class intervals; class intervals can be written in different ways and care is needed with the inequalities so an item (especially a boundary/minimum/maximum value) goes into the correct group; tally marks help avoid miscounts when filling in frequencies
learnerActions: Take a set of raw data (e.g. favourite sports of a class, or heights measured to the nearest cm) and count each value into its row using tally marks.
Convert the tallies to frequencies and check the frequencies sum to the total number of data points.
For continuous or wide-ranging numerical data, group into equal class intervals in inequality notation before tallying.
activities.intendedInsight: Tallying keeps counting accurate and reliable; frequencies should reconcile with the total, catching miscounts.

activities.title: Which chart fits? Decide, justify, and interpret comparatively
feedback: If you pick a line graph for favourite sports, note that categories have no ordering or continuity to join; a bar chart or pie chart fits categorical data.
If you report only one class's value when asked to compare, cite both data sets first, then state the difference as your conclusion.
When naming the modal class, pick the interval with the highest frequency, not the highest boundary number.
activities.rationale: Treating the representation as a choice keyed to data type, and pushing interpretation to a comparative conclusion, targets the two characteristic errors (wrong chart for type; read-off instead of conclusion). A sorting task, a selection item that includes an overlapping-boundary option, and a pie-angle computation contrasted with the 360÷frequency error can give a scorable check when anchored to concrete data sets, but such items do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a display.
sourceClaims: Representations should be chosen to fit the data type: categorical data is displayed with bar graphs/pie charts, while numerical (measurement) data uses displays with a measurement scale; distinguishing categorical from numerical data is foundational to choosing a display

KS3 pupils construct and interpret appropriate tables, charts and diagrams, including frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts and pictograms for categorical data, and vertical line (bar) charts for ungrouped and grouped numerical data
learnerActions: Sort several data sets by which display suits them: categorical → bar chart or pie chart; grouped continuous → touching bars/histogram; proportions of a whole → pie chart; genuine time-series → line graph.
For a categorical case (e.g. pupils' favourite sports), decide whether a line graph would be a good choice and explain why or why not.
Read a bar chart comparing Class A and Class B and state a CONCLUSION about the difference between the two data sets, citing both, not just one bar's value.
Given a grouped frequency table, name the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency).
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing a display is a judgement driven by data type, and interpreting a comparative chart means concluding about the difference between data sets, not reading a single value.

activities.title: Annotated reference: contrast displays side by side
feedback: If you cannot say why one chart's bars touch and the other's have gaps, re-read the data type: grouped continuous data has touching bars; categorical data (and ungrouped discrete values) has gaps between bars or lines.
Check your decision aid matches each data type to its display before using it to choose.
activities.rationale: A worked, annotated contrast is a useful reference and scaffold for the vocabulary and decision rules, though it does not let the learner set intervals or build and judge a representation — the discriminating skills. Use it alongside, not instead of, construction work.
sourceClaims: Representations should be chosen to fit the data type: categorical data is displayed with bar graphs/pie charts, while numerical (measurement) data uses displays with a measurement scale; distinguishing categorical from numerical data is foundational to choosing a display
learnerActions: Study a bar chart of categorical data (bars with gaps) set beside a histogram-style display of grouped continuous data (bars touching) and note what each tells you about the data type.
Examine a grouped frequency table in inequality notation and identify how the boundary value is assigned.
Reveal, for each chart type, which data type it suits and add that to a 'which chart?' decision aid.
activities.intendedInsight: The touching-versus-gapped bars distinction signals continuous versus categorical data; the notation shows where boundary values belong.

constraints: Assessment of understanding should include CONSTRUCTION (building a grouped frequency table and choosing/drawing a display), not only reading given charts; the construction step is what exposes the interval and representation judgements, and the curriculum requires pupils to construct as well as interpret.

Recognition-only or selection items can check interval and chart-choice decisions and catch specific errors (overlapping intervals; 360÷frequency), but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a display.
Static annotated displays are a reference/worked-example scaffold: they can label and contrast chart types but cannot let the learner set intervals or build and judge a representation.
Boundary values must be assigned by inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value belongs to exactly one class; intervals must cover the whole range without gaps.
Pie-chart sector angles are (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and must sum to 360°; dividing 360° by the frequency is a known error.
Reading a single value from a comparative chart is a performance slip to scaffold (underline the comparison, cite both data sets), not necessarily a conceptual gap; the reading skill may be intact.

3D versions of these inherently 2D displays can distort the proportions learners must read (e.g. perspective on a 3D pie chart), so a 2D display is the practical default for this topic. Comparative efficacy of 2D versus 3D is not established by the cited sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's framing that a line-graph-over-categories mismatch 'is seen, not told' and that dialogue/3D formats are unsuitable reflects catalog fit judgements; these have been softened to scoped affordances/limits rather than universal claims. A static image or a dialogue can still support learning; the objective limit retained is that recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction.
The constraint carrying the source's 3D 'adds nothing' claim was reworded to retain only the narrow distortion caution plus an efficacy caveat, dropping the categorical comparative claim.

Self-audit of worked figures: (frequency ÷ total) × 360° is the correct pie-angle formula and sectors summing to 360° is correct. Inequality-notation interval examples (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) correctly assign a boundary value of 10 to the second class. No arithmetic errors found in the source examples.

probeDeeper: 'Your intervals are 0-10 and 10-20 — where does a runner who took exactly 10 seconds go?' — forces the boundary/overlap issue into the open
Counterexample: 'Would a line graph be a good way to show pupils' favourite sports? Why or why not?' — tests chart-to-data-type on a categorical case
'Why did you choose intervals of width 10 rather than uneven widths?' — probes the equal-interval reasoning
'This chart shows Class A and Class B — what is your conclusion about the DIFFERENCE, not just one class?' — pushes interpretation to a comparative conclusion
assess.correctAnswer: Interpretation: names the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency) and draws a comparative CONCLUSION about the two classes, not a single bar's value. Construction: builds a grouped frequency table with equal, non-overlapping, gap-free class intervals in clear inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value has exactly one class, and chooses a representation that fits the data type — touching bars/histogram or a bar chart for the grouped frequencies (a pie chart if showing proportions), NOT a line graph joining classes. Unambiguous intervals and a chart matched to the data type are the discriminating moves.

errorPatterns.pattern: Overlapping or ambiguous class intervals: writes classes like 0-10, 10-20 (or leaves gaps) so a boundary value could belong to either class, or some values fall in none
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the tables prerequisite: use inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value — especially a boundary — belongs to exactly one class, and check the intervals cover the whole range without gaps
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On construction the child's intervals share endpoints without inequality notation (unsure where a value of exactly 10 goes) or leave gaps that omit values

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong representation for the data type: chooses a chart unsuited to the data — e.g. a line graph joining categorical bars, or a pie chart where the whole is not meaningful, or draws continuous grouped data as a bar chart with gaps like discrete categories
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach representation choice on the data-presentation prerequisite: match bars to categories, pie sectors to a meaningful whole, and joined lines to appropriately ordered measurements. Address grouped continuous displays here using clearly specified class intervals; do not send all chart-choice errors to the now pie-only topic.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the choose-and-draw step the child selects a line graph for categorical data, or otherwise picks a display that doesn't match whether the data is categorical, grouped continuous, a proportion, or a time-series

errorPatterns.pattern: Pie angle = 360 ÷ frequency: computes each sector angle by dividing 360° by the frequency instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the proportion on the pie-chart prerequisite: the angle is (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Check each sector against its category share, then check that the angles total a full turn; the sum alone does not establish that the shares are correct.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: If a pie chart is chosen, the child writes 360 ÷ frequency for a sector and the sectors do not sum to 360°

errorPatterns.pattern: Read-off instead of conclusion: on a comparative chart reads a single class/bar value where a conclusion about the difference between data sets is asked
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: underline the comparison in the question and have the child cite BOTH data sets before concluding; the reading skill is intact
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On interpret (b) the child states one class's or one bar's value rather than comparing the two data sets and concluding about the difference

responseLevels.gap: Constructs tables with overlapping/gappy or ambiguous intervals; chooses charts unsuited to the data type; reads a single value where a comparison is asked
responseLevels.full: Interprets given representations AND constructs a grouped frequency table with equal, non-overlapping intervals and selects a representation appropriate to the data type, justifying the choice — transferring to a fresh data set
responseLevels.partial: Interprets given tables and charts, and can draw a pie or bar chart when told which to use, but chooses class intervals or the representation unreliably when left to decide — can build a display but not judge which fits the data type

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two moves. FIRST, interpret given representations: (a) 'Here is a grouped frequency table of pupils' heights — which is the modal class?' (b) 'This bar chart compares Class A and Class B's scores — what can you conclude about the difference?' THEN, translate/construct: 'Here is the raw data — the times, to the nearest second, of 30 runners. Make a grouped frequency table (choose your own class intervals), then decide the best chart to display it and draw it.' Watch especially the class-interval boundaries and the chart choice — that construction step is the discriminator.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret step can be done fairly mechanically; the CONSTRUCT step forces the two judgements into the open. A child who doesn't grasp grouping writes overlapping or gappy intervals and cannot say where a boundary value goes; a child who doesn't grasp representation reaches for a chart that mismatches the data type (a line graph over categories). Both are visible in what they build, separating those who can read a display from those who can design one for the data.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Bar graphs
topic.description: Interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs
evidence: Read a time graph showing temperature changes over a day
Present data about plant growth over weeks as a time graph
Explain the difference between a bar chart (discrete) and a time graph (continuous)
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} choose the right type of chart for some data — for example, a bar chart for favourite colours or a line graph for temperature over a week — and draw it correctly?

pedagogy.summary: At 8-9, children learn to match the GRAPH TYPE to the DATA TYPE: discrete data (separate categories, counted) belong in a bar chart with gaps between bars; continuous data (measured, changing over time — temperature through a day, plant height over weeks) belong in a time graph whose points are joined because values exist in between. The NC Year 4 step is presenting discrete and continuous data 'using appropriate graphical methods'. The load-bearing ideas are (1) the discrete/continuous distinction drives the representation, (2) a time graph's line carries values BETWEEN the plotted points, and (3) the vertical scale must be checked before judging how big a change is. Teaching should contrast the two graph types on real data and read time graphs both at and between points.
bestPractices: Decide the graph type from the data type: counted categories → bar chart (bars separated); measured-over-time → time graph (points joined)
Read time graphs both at plotted points AND between them, naming that the line shows continuous change (interpolation)
Always read the vertical scale before describing a change, so a steep-looking line isn't over-read
Contrast a bar chart and a time graph of related data side by side so the difference in what each shows is explicit
keyRepresentations: Bar chart with separated bars (discrete categories)
Time graph / line graph with joined points (continuous change)
Paired display: the same context shown both ways to expose which fits
Axis with a clearly marked, even vertical scale
commonMisconceptions: Chooses the wrong representation for the data type — separate bars for continuous time data, or joins discrete category bars into a line
Believes a time graph only tells us the values at the plotted points, not in between (misses continuity)
Reads a steep line as a big change without checking the vertical scale (misleading-scale effect)
Reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation rather than as values against axes

learn.summary: For ages 8-9, learners decide which graph type fits which data type and read time graphs both at and between plotted points. Discrete data (counted, separate categories) belong in a bar chart with gaps between bars; continuous data are measured quantities, and when a measurement changes over time (temperature through a day, plant height over weeks) it fits a time/line graph whose points are joined because real values exist between them. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) the discrete/continuous distinction drives the choice of representation, (2) a joined line gives estimated values BETWEEN the plotted points (interpolation), which assumes the quantity changed fairly steadily between readings, and (3) the vertical scale must be read before judging how big a change is. Teaching contrasts the two graph types on related real data and reads time graphs at AND between points.

activities.title: Dual-view grapher: choose the graph that fits the data
feedback: If a learner joins the tops of the category (pet) bars: ask what a point halfway between cats and dogs would mean; since there is no pet 'between' cats and dogs, the joined line carries no meaning here — separated bars fit counted categories.

If a learner says the temperature at 10:30 cannot be known exactly, agree that it was not measured, then trace along the line between the 10:00 and 11:00 points and read an estimate there; name that temperature changes continuously, so in-between times do have values, and the line gives a sensible estimate if the temperature changed steadily between readings.
If a learner sorts first into counted-categories vs measured-over-time, confirm: counted → bars with gaps, measured-over-time → joined line.
activities.rationale: Contrasting the two graph types on related data and reading a time graph between points makes the discrete/continuous distinction and interpolation concrete. A draggable vertical guide reading any time (including between marks) is an optional interaction that makes continuity visible; a learner-chosen representation forces the data-type decision rather than recognising a given graph.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs, and begin to relate graphical representation to recording change over time
learnerActions: Take a data set and choose whether to show it as separated bars or a joined line.
For 'favourite pets' (counted categories, e.g. cats and dogs) choose bars with gaps; for 'classroom temperature through the day' choose a joined line.
When tempted to join category values, ask yourself: 'what would a point BETWEEN cats and dogs mean?' and notice there is no sensible answer.
For the temperature line, drag a vertical guide to estimate the value at a time that was never actually recorded, e.g. 10:30, between the plotted points.
Say out loud why the line makes sense for temperature but not for pet categories, using the words discrete and continuous.
activities.intendedInsight: A joined line only makes sense when in-between values are real — that is exactly what continuous data means; counted categories have no in-between, so they go in separated bars.

activities.title: Check the scale before calling a change 'big'
feedback: If a learner calls a change 'huge' from steepness while the axis spans only a few degrees: have them read the axis values and restate the change as an actual amount.
Show the same data on two axes; if the learner sees the lines differ, ask what actually changed (only the scale, not the data).
activities.rationale: Reading the vertical scale first guards against the misleading-scale effect; comparing stretched vs compressed axes of identical data makes the effect explicit.
sourceClaims: Students should be aware that changing the scale of the vertical axis affects the perception of growth — increasing the spacing between increments can make growth appear faster than it was
learnerActions: Look at a temperature line that appears steep and, before describing the change, read the numbers on the vertical axis.
Compare the same temperature data drawn on a stretched (widely spaced) vertical axis and on a compressed one; notice the line looks dramatic or gentle while the data is identical.
Optionally use a scale slider that stretches or shrinks the vertical axis of the same data to feel how the apparent size of the change changes.
State the actual size of the change in degrees, not just 'huge' from the steepness.
activities.intendedInsight: Steepness alone is misleading: the spacing of the vertical scale changes how big a change looks, so you must read the scale before judging the size of a change.

activities.title: Interpret a real time graph at and between points
feedback: If a learner plots plant-growth-over-weeks as unconnected bars, or draws a line through four fruit values, sort the data again as counted-categories vs measured-over-time and reconnect to the discrete/continuous vocabulary.
Probe: 'if I joined the tops of the fruit bars with a line, would the line mean anything?' to test the discrete/continuous boundary.
Probe: 'this line looks steep — what should you check before saying the temperature shot up?' to surface scale-checking.
activities.rationale: Interpreting on an actual time graph plus translating a real data table into the right chart together separate genuine understanding from surface graph-drawing: interpolating on continuous data and choosing bars for discrete data are the two discriminating moves.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs, and begin to relate graphical representation to recording change over time
learnerActions: Read a time graph of classroom temperature through one day: state the temperature at a marked time, and estimate it at an unmarked time such as 10:30 by reading between points.
Describe what a falling section after 3pm tells you about the situation (temperature getting cooler over time).
Then take a table of how many children chose each of four fruits and decide which graph to draw; draw separated bars against an even scale.
Explain in words why a joined line is right for temperature but a bar chart is right for the fruit choices.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting continuous data means estimating values between points and reading rising/falling as change over time; choosing bars for discrete categories and lines for measured-over-time shows the data type drives the representation.

activities.title: Annotated time graph as a reference scaffold
feedback: Use the annotations to confirm vocabulary, then move to a graph where you read an unmarked time yourself.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotation supports vocabulary and orientation. As a fixed reference it does not provide a dynamic read-out at an unmarked time or let the learner change the scale (a learner can still estimate between points by eye), so it should precede, not replace, interactive reading.
learnerActions: Tap parts of a static, annotated time graph to reveal what the axes, points and line mean.
Use it to recall the labels for a plotted point, the joined line (continuous change), and the vertical scale.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled time graph helps name the parts, but as a fixed image it does not give a draggable, precise read-out at an unmarked time or let you restretch the vertical scale; a learner can still estimate a value between points by eye, while an interactive graph makes reading any time and testing scale effects directly manipulable.

constraints: The annotated-graph activity is a reference scaffold: a fixed graph can label the parts but does not provide a dynamic read-out for an unmarked value or let the learner restretch the scale, so pair it with activities where the learner reads between points and compares axes.
Choosing and constructing the representation must stay a learner action: recognising a pre-chosen graph does not elicit the independent decision of which graph fits the data type.
Keep real data types concrete (counted categories vs measured-over-time); the discrete/continuous distinction only lands when learners sort actual data, not abstract definitions.
Interactions such as a draggable vertical guide, a scale slider, or linked stretched/compressed axes are optional ways to make continuity and scale concrete, not required mechanisms.
Keep examples consistent within an activity: use favourite pets (cats/dogs) for the dual-view grapher's discrete case and the four-fruit table for the translating task, rather than blending them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source listed conversation and 3D artefacts as poor fits with rationales like 'dialogue offers nothing to read' and '3D adds nothing'. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources, so they were not carried into guidance as universal laws; the genuine point retained is only that this skill centres on reading and constructing graphs, and that recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction.

The source's 'ideal' framing that live manipulation is the best way to learn this is a catalog preference, not established by the cited sources; retained as an interactive proposal with stated affordances, not as proof of superiority.

The reference-scaffold limitation was narrowed: a fixed graph lacks a dynamic read-out and scale-restretching, but a learner can still estimate between-point values by eye — stating a fixed graph 'cannot interpolate' would overstate the limit and undercut the continuity principle.

The original candidate blended 'favourite fruits/pets' and contradicted itself ('value between two fruits' vs 'no fruit between cats and dogs'); this is kept corrected to use pets consistently in the grapher activity, with fruits reserved for the translating task.

Translating: chooses a BAR chart for the discrete fruit categories (separated bars) — not a line — and draws it against an even scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Chooses the wrong representation for the data type — draws a joined line for discrete categories, or separated bars for continuous time data
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort the data as counted-categories vs measured-over-time first; counted → bars with gaps, measured-over-time → joined line; reconnect to the discrete/continuous vocabulary
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child draws a line through the four fruit values, or plots plant-growth-over-weeks as unconnected bars

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a time graph only tells the values at the plotted points, not between them (misses continuity)

errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked the temperature at 10:30 (between marks) the child says it can't be known

assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands reads a time graph between points and picks the representation from the data type; a child who doesn't says the temperature at 10:30 is unknowable, or draws a joined line for the discrete fruit data. The two moves — interpolating on continuous data, and choosing bars for discrete — together separate real understanding from surface graph-drawing.

pedagogy.summary: Read time and value axes together to solve line-graph comparison, difference and appropriate sum problems. Separate point height from change across equal time intervals; graph shape is not a literal picture of the situation. Temperature readings support trend interpretation and approximate interpolation under an explicit straight-line model. Period totals, such as monthly rainfall, can be compared and added but cannot be interpolated as rainfall at an intermediate date. Teach literal reads before combining values and interpreting trends.
bestPractices: Anchor the graph in a clear quantity, units and observation schedule; distinguish temperature observations from rainfall totals over periods.

Explicitly teach the three-part reading progression (Curcio): first READ THE DATA (lift a value straight off a point), then READ BETWEEN THE DATA (compare two points, find a difference, read an intermediate value), then READ BEYOND (predict the next day) — and name which you are asking for

Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE deliberately: pair 'which day was warmest?' (height) with 'which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) on the same graph, so children cannot conflate the tallest point with the biggest jump
Trace vertically from a plotted point to the time axis, then horizontally from that same point to the value axis; say the paired reading.
Read an intermediate temperature from the segment as a straight-line estimate; distinguish this model assumption from what was measured.

Contrast a genuine time-series (temperature) with data that should NOT be joined into a line (favourite fruit) so children learn that joined lines suit values ordered in time, such as temperature readings or monthly totals, whereas unordered categories should not be joined
keyRepresentations: Temperature-over-a-week line graph (the canonical continuous time-series for this age)

A crosshair / ruler slid along the line to read plotted values and to estimate values between plotted temperature observations under a straight-line assumption (makes interpolation visible as an estimate)
Paired axes with a right-angle trace from point to time-axis and to value-axis
Two questions side by side on one graph — 'highest point' vs 'steepest climb' — to physically separate height from change
A rising / flat / falling segment triad annotated as increase / no change / decrease
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture: reading the line's silhouette as a literal picture of the situation (a rising-then-falling temperature line 'is a hill/mountain', or a distance-time line read as the route travelled) rather than as a quantity plotted against time

Slope-height / height-for-difference confusion: when asked how much a quantity changed, naming the highest point rather than the steepest segment; treating a higher point as 'faster' or 'more increase'
Treating a line-based estimate as an exact unmeasured observation, or refusing any estimate because only the plotted points were measured.
Accepting or interpreting a joined line for categorical data (favourite pet) as if it showed a trend, or reading a scaled axis by counting squares rather than by the scale interval

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, solve comparison, sum and difference problems from line graphs. Read each point using both axes and the labelled scale; distinguish the highest observed value from the largest increase over equal time intervals. Use temperatures for reading and differences, and quantities that can meaningfully be added, such as monthly rainfall totals, for sum problems. Interpolated temperatures are estimates under a stated straight-line assumption, not additional measurements. Joining monthly rainfall totals does not reveal rainfall on intermediate dates.

activities.title: Read values and estimate between temperature observations
feedback: If you tap the tallest point for 'warmed up the most', that tells you the warmest day, which may or may not be where the biggest change happened — look instead for the segment that climbs most steeply across a single day.

If you read a value without tracing to both axes, pause: put your finger on the point, go straight down to read the day, then from the point go straight across to read the temperature, and say the pair.

The drawn segment passes smoothly through in-between values. Those are estimates assuming a straight-line change between readings; actual temperatures may have fluctuated differently, so this is not a record of every intervening temperature.
activities.rationale: Reading a time-series is a doing skill — lift a value, read between two values, find a difference, interpret a rise. Letting the learner act and the graph respond is intended to make interpolation and the slope-vs-height distinction concrete. A draggable/sliding read-out is one proposed way that may make the continuity of the segment visible; a ruler slid along a printed graph achieves a similar effect. Efficacy of the specific interaction is untested here.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed

KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Use a temperature-over-a-week line graph with observations at the same time each day and equal daily spacing. Slide a ruler, crosshair or finger along a segment to read a straight-line estimate between observations.

Slide between Monday and Tuesday and say aloud the values the line passes through — e.g. 14, 15, 16 degrees — noticing that the line gives estimated in-between values, not only the measured values at the plotted dots.

For each point, trace it back to BOTH axes: finger on the point, drop straight down to the time axis to read the day, then go back to the point and slide horizontally across to the value axis to read the temperature; say the paired coordinate.
Use a 'find the difference' move: mark two points and read the vertical gap between them (e.g. the rise from Tuesday to Wednesday).
Take on the challenge 'Which day did it warm up the MOST?' — then check whether the warmest day (tallest point) is the same as, or different from, the day of the steepest climb.
activities.intendedInsight: On this temperature graph, plotted points are observations and the connecting segments provide straight-line estimates between them. Compare rises over equal daily intervals to distinguish change from the temperature at a point.

activities.title: Separate HEIGHT from CHANGE on one graph
feedback: If you name the warmest day for 'warmed up the most', check the arrows — the longest upward arrow marks the biggest rise, which may not sit at the tallest point.
Correct justification sounds like 'it climbed 5 degrees from Monday to Tuesday', not 'that one is the highest'.
If height and steepest always seem to be the same day for you, try the tricky case where they come apart.
activities.rationale: Pairing a height question with a change question on the same graph targets height-for-difference confusion, a documented substitution error; comparing arrow lengths makes 'how much it changed' a visible, measurable quantity distinct from the tallest point.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed
learnerActions: On a single temperature line graph, answer 'Which day was warmest?' (height) and 'Which day did it warm up the most?' (steepest rise) — treat them as two different questions.
Draw a small vertical arrow for the change between each pair of consecutive days, pointing up for a rise and down for a fall, then compare the lengths of the upward arrows to find the biggest rise.
Justify your 'warmed up the most' answer by saying how far the line climbed across that one day, not by which point is highest.

Try a tricky case: a graph where a huge jump happens early in the week and the highest point is reached later by only a small rise, so the tallest point and the steepest segment are clearly on different days — identify each.
activities.intendedInsight: A higher observed temperature is not the same as a bigger increase. Over these equal one-day intervals, the largest rise has the steepest rising segment; with unequal intervals, compare changes and rates separately.

activities.title: Read the data, between the data, and beyond the data
feedback: For a difference question, report the gap (e.g. rose 3 degrees), not the two raw values; for a total/sum question, add the two read-off values and report the combined amount.

An intermediate point on the drawn temperature segment gives a straight-line estimate. Read it consistently with the axes and explain that the actual unmeasured value could differ; an exactly known temperature cannot be recovered from two daily observations alone.
A prediction is a reasoned guess from the trend; being off from the revealed value is fine — explain what the trend suggested.
activities.rationale: Curcio's three hierarchical levels structure the questions from literal lift to comparing/combining/finding differences to inference; this is where comparison, sum and difference problems from the graph live. Predict-then-reveal exercises reading beyond the data and makes the continuity of the line matter.
sourceClaims: Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment

KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Read the data: lift a single value straight off a marked point (e.g. the warmest day's temperature).

Read between the data: compare two observed values, find their difference, and combine values only where the quantity makes a meaningful total, such as rainfall totals for March and May. Do not add daily temperatures as if they were a total temperature. On a temperature line graph, separately estimate an intermediate value under the straight-line assumption.

Read beyond the data: hide the final plotted day (e.g. Friday on a Monday-to-Friday graph), predict and place it from the earlier trend, then reveal the real value and compare — discuss why the prediction may differ.
Each time, name which kind of reading you are doing: reading a value, reading between, or predicting.
activities.intendedInsight: Graph comprehension has a progression — you must read a value before you can compare, combine or find differences between values, and only then predict or infer — and naming which you are doing clarifies the task.

activities.title: When should data be joined into a line? Continuous vs categorical
feedback: A point between two temperature observations has a time and a line-based estimate. The true temperature at that time was not measured by this graph and need not match the estimate.
If you would join favourite-fruit counts with a line, ask: what would a point halfway between apple and banana mean? There is no in-between fruit category — so the counts should not be joined.
activities.rationale: Contrasting temperature observations with unordered categorical counts may help learners explain when joining points supports a meaningful interpretation. Temperature interpolation remains a model-based estimate; this proposed comparison is not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Compare a genuine time-series (temperature across days) with categorical data (favourite fruit) and decide which should be drawn as a joined line and which should not.
Run a finger along a temperature segment, naming the estimates it passes through ('the line estimates about 15 here'); distinguish these from temperatures actually measured at the plotted points.
Explain why joining 'favourite fruit' counts into a line would be meaningless — there is no continuous quantity between the categories.
activities.intendedInsight: A line joining temperature observations can show a trend and support estimates under an explicit interpolation assumption. Joining unordered fruit categories does not create a meaningful intermediate category; use bars for those counts.

activities.title: Confront the graph-as-picture habit
feedback: Describing the silhouette ('it went up and over') is the picture trap — switch to values: 'on Wednesday it was 18, on Thursday it fell to 14'.
A falling segment means the quantity decreased (it got colder), not that something physically went downhill.
activities.rationale: The graph-as-picture error persists even when a learner can describe the changes verbally, so directly re-reading point-by-point and tracing to axes aims to break the habit of treating the silhouette as the situation.
sourceClaims: Graph-as-picture error: students treat the graph as a literal picture of the problem situation (drawing/reading a hill shape for a speed-vs-time graph over a hill), with two subtypes — global correspondence (whole scene matched to whole graph) and feature correspondence (a local visual feature matched to a graph feature); this occurs even when the student can describe the changes verbally
learnerActions: If you catch yourself describing the line as 'a hill' or 'the route it travelled', cover the whole line and expose one point at a time.
For each exposed point, answer 'What does THIS point tell us?' and trace it to both axes, reading a day and its temperature.
Re-read the whole graph as a set of day/temperature pairs rather than a shape or a scene.
activities.intendedInsight: The line is a quantity plotted against time, not a literal picture of the event; each point is a paired coordinate, and the overall shape summarises how the value changed, not a landscape.

activities.title: Check questions and reading the scale correctly
feedback: If your answer is off by a consistent factor (e.g. you say 6 where each square is 2 degrees and the real answer is 12), you counted squares instead of using the scale — relabel the interval and re-read.

The highest temperature and largest one-day rise can occur together or on different days. Compare consecutive values over equal daily intervals before deciding; do not automatically reject the highest point.
activities.rationale: Comparison, difference, sum and ordering questions give a scorable check of the reading procedure, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner's own interpolation or justification, so keep producing-and-explaining tasks too. Scale mis-reading is a counting slip, not a conceptual gap, and is addressed by labelling the scale interval first. Any illustration should be schematic rather than requiring an exact drawn quantity to be eyeballed.
sourceClaims: Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment
learnerActions: Answer scorable items: choose the warmest day; estimate an intermediate temperature off a marked line (a sensible range is accepted); fill in 'the difference between March and May rainfall is ___ mm'; order months by rainfall.
Include one item that pairs 'highest point' against 'biggest rise' so you must distinguish height from change.
Before reporting any value, ask 'How much is each square worth here?' and label the scale interval, then read by the scale — not by counting squares as if each were one unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Targeted questions can check your reading skill, but you must read values by the axis scale interval, not by counting grid squares.

constraints: This topic assesses reading and solving problems from line graphs. Constructing a complete graph is developed separately in the later Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp); do not require unrelated bar-chart tasks as evidence of this objective.

Always trace values back to BOTH axes (from the point, go vertically to the time axis to read the time, and horizontally from the point to the value axis to read the value) to counter reading the line as a shape rather than paired coordinates.

Deliberately pair a height question ('which day was warmest?') with a change question ('which day warmed up the most?') on the same graph so learners cannot conflate the tallest point with the biggest jump.

For temperature observations joined by straight segments, read intermediate estimates aloud and name the straight-line assumption. The line does not establish the exact path taken between observations. Do not interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall on intermediate dates.

A labelled or tap-to-reveal graph can support a worked example. Ask the learner to read and explain new values before revealing answers when independent reading is the aim; paper tracing, discussion and digital controls are optional ways to organize this.

Recognition-only or pre-revealed items can confirm a classification or choice but do not themselves elicit the learner's own reading, difference-finding, combining/totalling, interpolation, or justification; include tasks where the learner produces and explains answers.
Scorable check items should use schematic illustrations and must not require eyeballing an exact drawn quantity that isn't readable from the scale.
Scale mis-reading is a counting slip to scaffold (label the interval, re-read), not a reason to reteach the whole graph concept.

For unordered categories such as favourite fruit, use bars rather than a joined trend line. Line graphs can also plot ordered period totals, but joining monthly totals does not supply rainfall amounts at intervening dates.

Where a point-only (intermediate-values-don't-exist) misconception appears, reteaching the continuous meaning may draw on the prerequisite micro-topic (continuous vs categorical data) rather than re-teaching the whole graph idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labels conversation/persona and 3D treatments as poor fits, asserting a third spatial dimension 'conveys nothing' and that a conversational wrapper 'could not verify' reading. These are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources and are omitted as universal laws. Narrowly scoped, observable concerns remain worth noting: a time-series is a two-variable (time vs quantity) plot, so an added spatial dimension does not correspond to a variable here and may invite the graph-as-picture error; and a purely decorative conversational wrapper would still need a live graph to check reading. These are affordance observations, not proof that any medium 'cannot teach'.
The original feedback marked the tallest point wrong for biggest rise. This is not generally valid: the highest temperature and largest rise may coincide, so each graph must be checked.
One cited source (Oak National Academy KS2 line-graph guidance) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as curriculum guidance of unconfirmed verification.

Draggable crosshair, live recolouring (steepest segment lighting up), and predict-then-drag are optional interaction examples that may make continuity and the height-vs-change distinction concrete; paper equivalents (sliding a ruler, drawing arrows) are acceptable, and these specific interactions are not required or proven mechanisms.
The original summary and evidence include SUM/total problems; a combine/total task was added to the read-between activity so this is genuinely delivered rather than only promised.
Taxonomy alignment repair after os-taxonomy PR #30 (2026-10-19). Sources were reused without being re-fetched. Activities are proposals, not empirically validated interventions.
The temporary bar-graph activities introduced to match the former description have been removed. PR #30 corrected the description to match the original line-graph evidence and assessment.

probeDeeper: Why is Friday warmest even though Monday–Tuesday has the biggest rise?
Could the actual temperature halfway between observations differ from 17°C? Explain the assumption behind the estimate.
Why can January and March rainfall totals be added, while daily temperatures are not a total temperature?
How would a value axis marked every 2°C change the way you read a point?
assess.correctAnswer: Friday is warmest at 19°C; Tuesday to Wednesday rises by 2°C; Monday to Tuesday has the largest daily rise, 4°C, although Friday is highest. Halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon the straight-line estimate is 17°C; the actual unmeasured temperature may differ. January plus March rainfall is 45 mm and February exceeds January by 15 mm. Wednesday to Thursday falls by 1°C, meaning the temperature decreased (it got colder), not that something went downhill. Both traces start at the plotted point: vertically to time and horizontally to value. Do not total daily temperatures or interpolate monthly rainfall totals as rainfall at an intermediate date.

errorPatterns.pattern: Graph-as-picture: reads the line's shape as a literal picture of the situation rather than a quantity over time ('it goes up like a hill then down the other side', or describes it as a route/mountain) instead of talking about temperature values on days

errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by putting 'highest point' and 'biggest jump' side by side on the same graph: mark the change between each pair of consecutive days with a little vertical arrow, and compare arrow lengths so the steepest rise is seen to differ from the tallest point
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child points to the warmest day (same point as task 1) and says 'that one, it's the highest', instead of the day with the biggest jump from the day before

errorPatterns.pattern: Scale mis-read: on task (1) or (2) counts grid squares as if each were one unit instead of reading the scale interval, giving a value or difference that is off by the scale factor

responseLevels.full: Reads values by the scale, distinguishes highest from largest rise, solves the rainfall sum/difference, explains a falling segment as a decrease in temperature and explains interpolation as an assumption-based estimate; transfers the procedure to another graph.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give an equally spaced line graph of temperatures recorded at noon: Monday 12°C, Tuesday 16°C, Wednesday 18°C, Thursday 17°C, Friday 19°C. Ask the learner to (1) read the warmest day and value, (2) calculate the Tuesday-to-Wednesday change, and (3) identify the interval with the largest rise. (4) Ask for the estimated temperature halfway between Tuesday noon and Wednesday noon, explicitly assuming straight-line change. (5) Then show a line graph of monthly rainfall totals (January 20 mm, February 35 mm, March 25 mm); ask for January plus March and the February–January difference. (6) Return to the temperature graph and ask what the falling Wednesday-to-Thursday segment means. Watch the reading and calculations without supplying the answers.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The fixed data deliberately separate the highest point (Friday) from the largest rise (Monday–Tuesday). Watching axis traces, scale reading and subtraction distinguishes sound graph reading from guessing by shape. The estimate requires an explicit assumption; a learner is not marked wrong for adding that the exact unmeasured value is unknown, provided they give the 17°C straight-line estimate. The rainfall questions check a meaningful sum and difference, and explaining the Wednesday-to-Thursday fall checks that a falling segment is read as a decrease rather than a picture.

topic.description: Complete, read, and interpret information in tables, including timetables

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a timetable — like a train or bus timetable — to find out when a journey leaves, arrives, and how long it takes?

pedagogy.summary: At age 9-10 children read and complete real information tables — bus and train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and solve one- and two-step problems from them: find a departure time, work out a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two things carry the teaching. First, tracking a value to the intersection of the correct ROW and COLUMN, because dense timetables invite off-by-one-row/column reading. Second, and most characteristically, computing time DURATIONS correctly: children who read '10:50' and '11:20' tend to subtract the digits as if time were decimal (getting 0.70, or calling a 2:23 journey 'two point two three hours'), because minutes are base-60, not base-10. The remedy is to count on in minutes across the hour on a clock or number line, never to subtract clock readings as decimals. Keep every table anchored in a real purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.
bestPractices: Track every value to the ROW×COLUMN intersection explicitly — finger on the row, finger on the column, meet in the middle — to defeat off-by-one-row/column reading in dense timetables

Teach durations by COUNTING ON in minutes across the hour (10:50 → 11:00 is 10 min, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 min), using an empty number line or clock face — never by subtracting clock readings as if decimals

Confront the time-as-decimal habit head-on: when a child says a journey takes 0.70 or 2.23 hours, use an analogue clock to show 60 minutes in an hour so the digits after the colon are seen as minutes, not tenths
Underline the question words ('how long', 'how many more', 'how much later') so children compute the DIFFERENCE/DURATION asked for rather than reading a single value off the table
Read two-way tables by naming what each cell, row total and column total MEANS ('this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls') before doing any arithmetic
Anchor tables in an authentic task — catch the 8:40 bus, work out if you make the connection — so reading is purposeful rather than mechanical

A two-way table (e.g. sport × gender) with row and column totals shown
An empty number line or clock face for counting on the minutes of a duration across the hour
A finger/ruler trace from row and column to their intersection cell
