Reading off a single value when a difference or duration is asked ('how many more', 'how much longer') instead of computing it
Off-by-one-row/column reading: taking the value from an adjacent service or stop in a dense grid
In a two-way table, confusing a row/column TOTAL (a margin) with a single cell, or double-counting when categories overlap

learn.summary: For ages 9-10, teach children to read and complete real information tables — bus/train timetables and two-way tables (e.g. favourite sport by gender) — and to solve one- and two-step problems: find a departure time, compute a journey duration, complete a missing cell, compare two values. Two difficulties carry the teaching: tracking a value to the correct ROW×COLUMN intersection (dense grids invite off-by-one reading), and computing time DURATIONS by counting on in minutes across the hour rather than subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals. Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, plan the journey) so the numbers mean something.

activities.title: Live timetable with intersection highlighting
feedback: If the answer belongs to a neighbouring row or column, re-trace: one finger on the row, one on the column, and read only where they meet; use a ruler edge to isolate the row in a crowded timetable.
If a duration comes out as 0.70 or '70', re-count the jumps: to the next o'clock first (10:50→11:00 = 10 min), then past it (→11:20 = 20 min), total 30 minutes.

If the answer is only slightly out (e.g. a jump miscounted, or a boundary minute counted twice when counting minute by minute), the counting-on approach is likely sound — have them re-mark the jumps on a number line and re-add rather than reteaching the concept.
activities.rationale: Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the two hardest parts of this skill, and making them felt through tracing and counting-on targets the specific off-by-one and time-as-decimal errors. Optional live highlighting and a minute-track are concrete ways to make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
learnerActions: Use a real bus/train timetable (often services in columns and stops in rows, but check the headings because layouts vary) to find when a named service reaches a named stop.

Track the stop-row with one finger and the service-column with the other, meeting at the intersecting cell. If a screen model is available, tapping a row and column can light up ONLY the intersecting cell so the off-by-one habit has nowhere to hide.

Find a journey duration by counting on in minutes across the hour: 10:50 → 11:00 is 10 minutes, → 11:20 is another 20, so 30 minutes. If a duration tool is available, drag a marker along a minute-track and watch it tick across the hour.
State out loud why you cannot simply subtract 11:20 − 10:50 and call it 0.70 — the digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading tables is a doing skill on a 2D grid: values live at a row×column intersection, and time durations are counted in minutes across the hour, not subtracted as decimals.

activities.title: Confront time-as-decimal with an analogue clock
feedback: If the child still subtracts digits, return to the clock: show the 60 minutes in the hour and count the jumps to and past the o'clock.
Check the 14:45 + 40 min answer: 14:45→15:00 is 15 min, then 25 more to 15:25.
Check the 'next service 25 minutes later' answer: from 10:50, count 10:50→11:00 is 10 min, then 15 more to 11:15, so it leaves at 11:15.
activities.rationale: The source names reading clock times as decimals as a known misconception and names the analogue clock plus 'how many minutes in an hour' as the remedy, so this activity confronts the habit directly and rehearses it across the hour in both directions.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour
learnerActions: When a journey duration has been found by subtracting clock times as if they were decimals (e.g. 11:20 − 10:50 written as 0.70, or '70 minutes'), look at an analogue clock and state how many minutes are in one hour (60).
Find the correct duration in minutes by counting on from the start time to the end time across the hour on the clock face or an empty number line (e.g. 10:50 → 11:00 → 11:20 = 30 minutes).
Try a journey that crosses the hour in the other direction too — e.g. a train leaving at 14:45 with a 40-minute journey: when does it arrive?
Combine a lookup with a forward duration: if the next service is 25 minutes later than the one shown (say it leaves at 10:50), count on to find its departure time rather than adding digits.
activities.intendedInsight: The digits after the colon are minutes out of 60, not tenths of an hour, so durations must be counted in minutes, not read as decimals.

activities.title: Complete and interpret a two-way table
feedback: If the child reports a single cell (e.g. the number of girls who chose football) when a difference was asked, re-read the underlined 'how many MORE' and point to both values before subtracting.

If a margin total is confused with a single cell, name each number's meaning again before arithmetic. (In a sport-by-gender table the categories do not overlap; keep the double-counting caution for tables where a child could be counted in more than one category.)
activities.rationale: The source names reading off a single value when a difference is asked as a misconception, with underlining the question words as the remedy; naming cells vs totals first targets margin-vs-cell confusion.
sourceClaims: When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
learnerActions: Before any arithmetic, name what each cell, row total and column total MEANS (e.g. 'this cell is girls who chose football; this end number is all the girls').

Complete a missing cell in a two-way table of favourite sport by gender from the given data, checking the filled cell against its row and column totals. If a screen model is available, row and column totals can update live so a filled cell can be checked against its margins.
Answer a 'how many more' question — underline the question words, point to BOTH values, and show the subtraction.
Contrast with a plain 'how many' question so the difference between reading one value and computing a difference is explicit.
activities.intendedInsight: A cell, a row total and a column total mean different things; 'how many more' asks for a difference between two values, not a single read-off.

activities.title: Scorable checks on lookups, durations and cell completion
feedback: A cross-the-hour duration item surfaces decimal subtraction (0.70/'70') versus a correct 30 minutes — if wrong, return to counting on across the hour.
A 'how many more' item surfaces reading a single value instead of a difference — if wrong, point to both values and subtract.
activities.rationale: Lookups, durations and complete-the-cell tasks give a scorable check of the reading procedure; purposely including a cross-the-hour duration and a 'how many more' item catches the two named misconceptions. This format checks a recognition/completion response and does not by itself elicit the child's independent counting-on method, so pair it with the watched performance task.
sourceClaims: Children read digital/clock times as decimal numbers: from a bus timetable they compute a journey as '2.23' and say it takes 'two point two three hours', interpreting the digits after the point as a decimal fraction rather than minutes; the remedy is an analogue clock and discussing how many minutes are in an hour

When asked 'how many more' from a chart/table, children read off a single value (e.g. the number one child has) instead of computing the difference; underlining the question words 'how many more' helps direct attention to the required operation
learnerActions: Find a departure time from a shown timetable (selecting from options).
Complete 'the journey from A to B takes ___ minutes', including at least one item where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50→11:20).
Complete or fill a missing cell in a two-way table.
Answer one 'how many more' item that requires a difference, not a single value.
activities.intendedInsight: The reading-and-calculating procedure can be checked against items deliberately chosen to catch time-as-decimal and read-off-instead-of-difference errors.

activities.title: Annotated worked-example timetable (scaffold)
feedback: Once the parts are named confidently, move to a table the child completes and calculates on themselves — this annotated example lets the child recognise structure but does not itself let them perform a duration calculation or complete a table.
activities.rationale: A static annotated grid can label structure and reveal what a cell means, which is a useful orientation, but it pre-bakes answers and does not elicit the duration or completion skill. It is a worked example only, not a substitute for the child doing the calculation.
learnerActions: Study a labelled timetable grid where the structure is annotated: services vs stops and what a single time cell means (and, on a two-way table, a single cell vs a row or column total), with tap-to-reveal explanations of what each part means.
Use it to rehearse naming the parts before doing your own lookups and durations on a live table.
activities.intendedInsight: Understanding the grid structure (services, stops and cells in a timetable; cells and totals in a two-way table) supports accurate reading before the child performs lookups and duration calculations independently.

constraints: Durations must be taught by counting on in minutes across the hour (to the o'clock, then past it) on a clock face or empty number line — never by subtracting clock readings as if they were base-10 decimals.

A static annotated/tap-to-reveal timetable is a worked example only: it orients the child to structure but does not itself let them perform a duration calculation or complete a table, which are the actual skills.
Scorable multiple-choice/fill items check recognition and completion and do not by themselves elicit the child's independent counting-on method; pair them with a watched performance task.
Keep every table anchored in an authentic purpose (catch the bus, make the connection) so reading is meaningful rather than mechanical.
Prerequisites may need reteaching: time conversion/minutes-in-an-hour for duration errors, and careful grid reading for off-by-one-row/column errors.
The double-counting caution applies only to tables where a child could fall into more than one category; a mutually-exclusive table (e.g. sport by gender) does not overlap.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row ranked a conversational format and a third spatial dimension as poor fit for this flat-grid skill and described them as 'adds nothing'. They are dropped rather than asserted as universal pedagogical laws, since the catalog ranking does not establish comparative efficacy or necessity; a flat grid simply does not require a third spatial dimension for this content.

Arithmetic check: 10:50→11:00 = 10 min, →11:20 = 20 min, total 30 min (correct); 14:45 + 40 min = 15:25 (correct); 10:50 + 25 min = 11:15 (correct). The erroneous '0.70'/'70' results are retained only as the misconception to confront, never as valid answers.
Efficacy of optional live-highlight and minute-track interactions is not source-established; they are offered with 'if available'/'may help' wording.

The Year 5 curriculum source claim establishes that completing/reading/interpreting tables is appropriate content for this age but does not evidence any individual activity's mechanism rationale, so it is not cited within the activities; its placement support is reflected in the summary context only.

probeDeeper: 'The bus leaves at 10:50 and arrives at 11:20 — show me how you worked out the 30 minutes.' — forces the method into the open
'A train leaves at 14:45 and the journey is 40 minutes — when does it arrive?' — transfer across the hour in the other direction
'What does this number at the end of the row mean?' (a row total) — probes cell-vs-total understanding
'If the next bus is 25 minutes later than this one, what time does it leave?' — combines reading with a duration in a fresh direction
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) the child tracks the correct row and column to their intersection and reads the right time; for (2) they compute the duration by counting on in minutes across the hour (10:50→11:20 = 30 minutes), not by subtracting the digits; for (3) they complete the cell using the right row and column (checking against a total if available) and give the DIFFERENCE between girls and boys, not a single value. Tracking to the intersection and counting minutes in base-60 are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Time-as-decimal: computes a duration by subtracting or reading clock times as base-10 numbers — giving 0.70 for 10:50 to 11:20, or calling a journey '2.23 hours' — because minutes are treated as tenths rather than sixtieths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach duration on the time-conversion prerequisite: use an analogue clock and empty number line, establish 60 minutes in an hour, and count on 10:50→11:00→11:20 so the child sees the answer as minutes, not tenths
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child subtracts the digits (11:20 − 10:50 → '70' or '0.70'/'0.30') or reports the duration as a decimal number of hours, rather than counting minutes across the hour

errorPatterns.pattern: Read-off-instead-of-difference: when asked 'how many more' or 'how much longer', reads a single value straight off the table rather than computing the difference between two
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront in place: underline the question words 'how many MORE', and have the child point to BOTH values and show the subtraction; contrast with a plain 'how many' question to make the difference explicit
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the 'how many more girls than boys' part of task (3), the child states the number of girls who chose football (a single cell) instead of subtracting the boys' value

errorPatterns.pattern: Off-by-one-row/column reading: in a dense grid, takes the value from an adjacent service or stop — the correct kind of value but from the wrong intersection
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach careful grid reading on the tables prerequisite: track the row with one finger and the column with the other and meet at the intersection; use a ruler/edge to isolate the row in a crowded timetable
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child gives a plausible but wrong time that belongs to the neighbouring column/row, without tracking row and column to their meeting point

errorPatterns.pattern: Counting-on slip: uses the right count-on method for a duration but miscounts the minutes (e.g. counts the hour boundary twice), giving an answer a few minutes out
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have them re-mark the jumps on the number line (to the o'clock, then past it) and re-add; the concept is intact, only the count slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) the child's method is sound — counting on across the hour — but the total is off by a few minutes

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably find a departure time (reads the wrong row/column), and computes durations by treating clock times as decimals
responseLevels.full: Tracks values to the correct row×column intersection, computes durations by counting on in minutes across the hour, finds differences, completes and uses two-way table totals, and transfers the same reading to a fresh timetable unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual departure times and completes given cells correctly, but computes durations by decimal subtraction, or reads off a single value when a difference/duration is asked — reads the data but not between it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put a real bus or train timetable (services in columns, several stops in rows) and a partly-completed two-way table (e.g. favourite sport by gender, with some cells and one total missing) in front of the child. Set these tasks and WATCH how they do them, saying little: (1) 'Find the time the 9:15 service reaches [named stop].' (2) 'How long does the journey from [stop A] to [stop B] take on that service?' — choose stops where the arrival crosses the hour (e.g. 10:50 to 11:20). (3) 'Fill in the missing cell in this table, and tell me how many MORE girls than boys chose football.' (Set the task and WATCH — do not model the duration method or point to the right cell.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (2) is chosen to cross the hour, so a child treating time as decimal produces a visibly wrong duration (0.70, or '70') while a child counting on gives 30 minutes — the two reason to different answers on the same question. Task (3) pairs a straight lookup with a 'how many more', separating a child who reads the data from one who reads between it; and the two-way structure exposes row/column-total confusion that a single lookup would hide.

topic.name: Line graphs
topic.description: Construct and interpret line graphs for continuous data (e.g. temperature over time, plant growth); read intermediate values, identify trends, and solve comparison and difference problems
evidence: Read values from a line graph showing temperature over a day, including estimating between plotted points
Construct a line graph from a table of continuous data, choosing an appropriate scale and labelling axes correctly
Use a line graph to solve a two-step problem, such as finding the time period with the greatest rate of change
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} recorded the temperature outside every hour for a day, could they plot those readings on a line graph with proper labels — and then use it to answer questions like 'when was it warmest?' or 'how much did it drop between 3pm and 6pm?'

pedagogy.summary: Construct and interpret line graphs for a measured quantity changing over time. Build from the earlier line-graph problem-solving topic: select a scale, label axes and units, plot pairs accurately and connect observations in time order. Distinguish observations from straight-line estimates, and point height from change or rate. Require an independently produced graph as well as verbal interpretation.
bestPractices: Begin with a small familiar table and discuss the variables, units and observation times before drawing.
Choose evenly spaced numerical scales that include the data; label each axis and unit.
Plot every time/value pair, checking both coordinates before joining points in time order.
Introduce unequal time intervals only after equal intervals, preserving the numerical spacing of time.
Ask for a trend and a numerical difference, then for an intermediate estimate with its assumption.
keyRepresentations: A paired table and a pupil-constructed time/temperature graph.
Axes with equally spaced numerical intervals and visible units.
A straight segment between two observations labelled as a model-based estimate.
Two intervals showing why total change and change per hour can differ.
commonMisconceptions: Treats rows as equally spaced times when the time gaps differ.
Uses a changing numerical scale along an axis.
Swaps coordinates or reads graph height without the time/value units.
Treats a line segment as an exact record of every unmeasured value.
Names the highest point when asked for the largest change or fastest increase.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, construct a complete line graph from a table of continuous measurements and use it to answer questions. Choose labelled numerical scales, preserve actual time spacing, plot paired readings and join in order. Read observations, describe trends, compute differences and estimate between observations under an explicit straight-line assumption. With unequal intervals, distinguish total change from change per hour.

activities.title: Build a line graph from a table
feedback: If the points are equally spaced in value because each occupies a new row, read the temperature scale rather than counting rows.
If a label or unit is missing, ask what another reader would need to recover a table value.
If a plotted point disagrees with the table, check its two coordinates before redrawing the whole graph.
activities.rationale: The task elicits the construction performance required by the updated objective. The topic description and evidence statements establish scope; the activity is an editorial proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs and use these to solve problems (statutory statistics content for this age)
learnerActions: Use temperatures at 09:00 12°C, 10:00 16°C, 11:00 18°C, 12:00 17°C and 13:00 19°C. Name time as the horizontal variable and temperature as the vertical variable.
Choose equal-hour spacing and a vertical scale covering 12–19°C; a 0–20°C axis with equal 2°C intervals and clear minor divisions is one option. Label time and temperature (°C).
Plot each pair yourself, check its horizontal and vertical coordinates, join points in time order, and add an informative title.
Compare your plotted points with the table before viewing a worked answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A line graph is a constructed mapping between paired measurements and labelled numerical axes, not a copied silhouette.

activities.title: Read, compare and estimate on your graph
feedback: The highest point is 19°C at 13:00, but the largest hourly rise is 4°C from 09:00 to 10:00.
The 10:00–11:00 rise is 2°C; the straight-line estimate for 10:30 is 17°C, not a measurement.
Actual unmeasured temperature could have differed; a useful estimate is not an exact observation.
activities.rationale: Reading values before comparing or inferring moves from observation to interpretation and uses common height/shape confusions as teaching targets; it is a proposed activity, not an evaluated intervention.
sourceClaims: Graph-as-picture error: students treat the graph as a literal picture of the problem situation (drawing/reading a hill shape for a speed-vs-time graph over a hill), with two subtypes — global correspondence (whole scene matched to whole graph) and feature correspondence (a local visual feature matched to a graph feature); this occurs even when the student can describe the changes verbally

Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed

Curcio's three hierarchical levels of graph comprehension — reading the data (literal lift), reading between the data (compare/combine/find differences), reading beyond the data (predict/infer) — students must read the data before they can read between or beyond it; framework adopted by NCTM for assessment
learnerActions: Identify the highest recorded temperature and the interval with the largest increase.
Find the 10:00–11:00 change, then estimate 10:30 using the straight segment and state the assumption.
Explain a flat or falling segment in terms of the measured quantity; distinguish the line from a picture of a journey or landscape.
activities.intendedInsight: Point height, change and estimated intermediate values answer different questions.

activities.title: Keep unequal time intervals honest
feedback: If the three points are equally spaced along time, check the clock times and re-space them.
Compute both the change and elapsed time; 6 ÷ 2 = 3°C per hour.
activities.rationale: This transfer task extends the height-versus-change distinction to the rate-of-change evidence. It is proposed practice, not an evaluated lesson.
sourceClaims: Slope-height confusion and related substitutions (height-for-slope, slope-for-height, height-for-difference, slope-for-curvature): students use the wrong graphical feature for the quantity asked; McDermott et al. found as many as half of students used height instead of slope to judge speed
learnerActions: Plot a second table: 09:00 10°C, 10:00 14°C and 12:00 20°C. Make the 10:00–12:00 gap twice the 09:00–10:00 gap.
Compare the first rise, 4°C in one hour, with the later rise, 6°C in two hours. Calculate change per hour before saying which interval warmed faster.
Explain why the larger total increase is not necessarily the steeper rise when time intervals differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Numerical time spacing determines the plotted rate: 4°C per hour is faster than 3°C per hour although 6°C is the larger total rise.

activities.title: Explain when a line is useful
feedback: Joining unordered categories does not define a useful interpolation.
Time-ordered observations can support a line-based estimate only under a stated assumption about what happened between them.
activities.rationale: The bar/line contrast is used only to clarify when joining points is meaningful, without claiming that one representation is always superior; it is a proposed activity.
sourceClaims: KS2 line-graph teaching: line graphs are used for continuous data where points between plotted points carry meaning; a rising line means an increase, a falling line a decrease, a flat line no change; pupils read values and find differences from the graph
learnerActions: Compare a temperature table indexed by time with favourite-fruit counts by unordered category. Choose a line graph for the former and bars for the latter.
Explain what an intermediate time means, and why halfway between apple and banana has no corresponding ordered category value.
Check that your own graph could be read by someone who did not see the original table.
activities.intendedInsight: Graph choice depends on the variables and their ordering; connecting points does not manufacture meaningful intermediate data.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Line plots with fractions
topic.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); use operations on fractions to solve problems involving data in line plots (e.g. redistribute total equally)
evidence: Create a line plot showing lengths measured to the nearest 1/8 inch
Use the line plot to find the total of all measurements by adding fractions
Solve: 'If the total liquid were redistributed equally among all beakers, how much would each have?'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the lengths of several objects to the nearest quarter or eighth of an inch and plotted them on a number line, could they use those measurements to work out totals or share amounts equally?

pedagogy.summary: At age 10-11 children make a LINE PLOT of measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and then OPERATE on that data with fractions — totalling measurements, finding differences, and redistributing a total equally among the data points. Two ideas carry the teaching. First, a line plot is not a bar graph: its horizontal axis is a genuine MEASUREMENT SCALE (a number line), so every position on it exists whether or not a measurement falls there ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and gaps between observed values must be shown. Second, the signature problem — 'if the total were shared equally, how much would each have?' — is an informal, hands-on route to the MEAN (fair share), and to solve it children total the fractions (often re-labelling the scale in a common unit such as eighths to get like denominators) and then divide by the count. So the topic fuses data display with fraction arithmetic, and the equal-redistribution task quietly previews averaging.
bestPractices: Draw the horizontal axis as a proper measurement scale (a number line marked in the fractional unit), and include every position — mark unobserved values too, because unlike categories, measurement values have gaps that must be shown
Distinguish the line plot from a bar graph explicitly: the axis is a measurement scale you could read off a ruler, not a set of separate categories
Re-label the scale in a common fractional unit (e.g. eighths) so that totalling and comparing measurements produces like denominators
Treat 'redistribute the total equally' as a fair-share problem — pour everything together, then share among the data points — making the link to the mean concrete before it is named
Keep the fraction arithmetic (adding unlike denominators, dividing by the count) reliable, since the data questions depend on it
Attend to precision when measuring and recording to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8, and place each mark carefully at its scale position
keyRepresentations: A number-line measurement scale marked in eighths, with an X (or dot) stacked above each measured value — the line plot itself
The same measurements re-expressed over a common denominator (eighths) for totalling
A 'pour together then share equally' image for the equal-redistribution (fair-share/mean) task
A ruler marked in halves/quarters/eighths, showing where the scale of the plot comes from
commonMisconceptions: Treating a line plot like a bar graph — showing only the values that occur, side by side as categories, with no continuous scale and no gaps for unobserved values
Adding the measurement fractions by combining numerators and denominators instead of finding a common denominator
Not seeing 'redistribute equally' as total ÷ count (the fair share / mean) — giving a middle value or leaving the data unchanged
Placing marks imprecisely on the scale, or mis-reading the fractional interval (e.g. an eighth for a quarter)

learn.summary: Learners aged 10-11 make a line plot of measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8), then operate on that data with fractions: totalling measurements, finding differences, and redistributing a total equally among the data points. Two ideas carry the teaching. First, a line plot is not a bar graph: its horizontal axis is a genuine measurement scale (a number line), so every position on it exists whether or not a measurement falls there, and gaps between observed values must be shown. Second, the signature problem — 'if the total were shared equally, how much would each have?' — is an informal, hands-on route to the mean (fair share): learners total the fractions (often re-labelling the scale in a common unit such as eighths to get like denominators) and then divide by the count. The topic fuses data display with fraction arithmetic, and the equal-redistribution task (using identical containers so equal volume reads cleanly) previews averaging before it is named.

activities.title: Place-and-share: build the plot, then pour the total
feedback: If a mark lands on the wrong fractional interval (e.g. at 3/8 when the value is 1/2 = 4/8), point to a labelled position and count the eighths across to re-place it; the plot's structure is fine, only the placement slipped.
If observed values are drawn as adjacent bars with no empty positions between them, show a ruler: every eighth exists on the scale, so unobserved positions must stay visible as gaps.
If fractions are added by combining numerators and denominators (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/6), re-label both in eighths first (4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8) and check the sum against the scale.

If the fair share is answered with an unchanged amount, or by picking a middle or most common value without working, pour everything together to get the total, then share it among all the containers: equally means total ÷ count. (For 3/4, 1/2, 1/4, 1/2 the middle value happens to equal the fair share of 1/2, so ask to see the total-and-divide working rather than judging by the answer alone.)
activities.rationale: Placing marks on a real fractional scale and physically pouring-then-sharing is proposed to make the fill-the-gaps and fair-share ideas concrete and operable, rehearsing both the display skill and the fraction arithmetic the data questions depend on. An optional interactive version may let the learner drag each X onto the scale, auto-re-label amounts in eighths when totalling, and animate the pour-and-share so each container settles at the shared amount; these are illustrative mechanisms, not requirements — paper, a ruler and real identical beakers achieve the same work and may be preferable for measuring precision.
sourceClaims: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale

Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: Measure (or use given) several lengths to the nearest 1/8 and place a mark (an X or dot) above each value on a horizontal scale marked in eighths.
Keep every eighth-position on the scale visible, including positions where no measurement falls, so the gaps are shown (for example, if nothing lands on 4 5/8, that spot stays on the number line).
Say aloud why an unobserved value still has a place on the scale: it is a measurement value on a ruler-like scale, not a separate category.

For a fair-share task, start with four identical (same-size) containers holding 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/2 cup. Combine all the liquid into one larger container that can hold at least 2 cups, and write the sum, re-labelling each amount in eighths: 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups.
Pour the combined 2 cups equally back into the four identical containers and record how much each now holds; connect the result (1/2 cup each) to total ÷ count = 2 ÷ 4.
Total the two shortest measurements and find a difference between two values, re-expressing over a common denominator first.
activities.intendedInsight: A line plot's axis is a continuous measurement scale with gaps for unobserved values, not a row of categories; and 'share the total equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share, which previews the mean made physical.

activities.title: Check the operations on a given plot
feedback: For an answer that adds tops and bottoms (e.g. 1/2 + 3/4 giving 4/6), re-express both in eighths and recompute; 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8.
For a fair-share answer that is the most common amount or an unchanged value, re-total all amounts and divide by the number of containers.
If a difference is found without first making like denominators, re-express both values in eighths before subtracting, then check the result against the scale.
activities.rationale: A scorable check of totals, differences and the equal-share item verifies the fraction operations and the fair-share interpretation. This is a focused check on given data; it does not by itself require the learner to construct a plot from raw measurements, so pair it with the construction activity. As a design choice for this check, keep data sets small with clean fraction sums so the arithmetic stays reliable and the reasoning stays visible.
sourceClaims: Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: From a provided small line plot, write the total of the two shortest measurements, showing the common-denominator step.
Answer a fair-share question such as 'If all the liquid were shared equally between identical containers, how much would each hold?' by totalling then dividing by the count.
Compare two values to find a difference, re-expressing over eighths first.
Watch for and avoid two traps: adding numerators and denominators together, and reporting a middle value instead of total ÷ count.
activities.intendedInsight: Totals, differences and fair shares read off a line plot all depend on correct like-denominator fraction arithmetic and on reading 'equally' as total ÷ count.

activities.title: Explain and stretch the fair-share idea
feedback: If the learner says the empty spot should be removed, return to the ruler image: a measurement value is not a category, so its position exists regardless of whether data falls there.

If adding the zero container does not change the learner's answer, recompute total ÷ count with the new count (2 cups ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each): the fair share is sensitive to how many are sharing, even when the added amount is zero.
If the fruit bar chart and the line plot are treated as the same, point out that fruit names are categories with no scale, while lengths sit on a measurement number line.
activities.rationale: Explanation and counterexample probes surface whether understanding is robust and transfer the fair-share reasoning to a new case, including sensitivity to the count. Verbal explanation complements, but does not replace, the hands-on construction and computation; explaining a procedure is not the same as performing it.
sourceClaims: A line plot displays measurement data on a number-line diagram whose scale corresponds to the measuring tool; unlike categorical data on a bar graph, measurement values have gaps that must be shown ('64 inches is not a category like spiders'), and a value not present is still written in its proper position on the scale

Standard 5.MD.2: make a line plot in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and use fraction operations to solve problems, e.g. given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find how much each would hold if the total were redistributed equally — which Grade 6 students later see as the MEAN of the data set; solving such problems may require re-labelling the scale in eighths to produce like denominators
Adding fractions with unlike denominators requires replacing them with equivalent fractions over a common denominator (a well-documented error is adding numerators and denominators directly)
learnerActions: Answer: 'You didn't measure any item at 4 5/8 — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' to put the measurement-scale-vs-category distinction into words.
Explain why you changed both fractions into eighths before adding them.
Tackle a counterexample: 'If one more identical container with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' and state why the answer changes.
Contrast this line plot with a bar chart of favourite fruits and say what makes the axes different.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why unobserved positions remain on the scale, why common denominators are needed, and how the fair share responds to the count (including a zero) consolidates both the display and the averaging ideas.

constraints: Reliable fraction arithmetic (adding unlike denominators, dividing by a count) is a prerequisite the data questions depend on; shore it up if it is shaky.

The horizontal axis must be drawn as a proper measurement scale (an evenly spaced number line marked in the fractional unit) with every position present, including unobserved values shown as gaps — not a set of separate bar-graph categories.

A static annotated line plot can display the scale and label totals and fair shares as a reference or worked example, but it does not let the learner place data, show gaps, or carry out the pour-and-share, so it is a support rather than the main task.

An interactive drag/pour tool is one way to make the mechanism concrete; paper plots, a real ruler, and physical identical beakers accomplish the same learning and may be preferable for precision in measuring and recording. A 2D scene suffices for this measurement scale and its data.
A recognition-only or multiple-choice check can verify answers but does not by itself elicit construction of a plot from raw measurements; combine it with a construction task.
Role-play or in-character dialogue does not confirm that the learner can accurately place marks or perform the fraction arithmetic, so it is not a substitute for a do-and-calculate task.

Attend to precision: measure and record to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 and place each mark carefully at its scale position; distinguish a placement slip (scaffold) from a conceptual bar-graph error (reteach).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3/4 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/2 = 6/8 + 4/8 + 2/8 + 4/8 = 16/8 = 2 cups; shared among 4 gives 1/2 cup each (2 ÷ 4); adding a zero container gives 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5 cup each. The source example 4 3/8 + 4 1/2 = 8 7/8 inches also checks out (3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8), with 4 3/8 and 4 1/2 being the two shortest of the source pencil set. 1/2 + 3/4 = 4/8 + 6/8 = 10/8 = 1 2/8. These were checked during this review but not independently re-verified against the original sources.
'Identical beakers' was restored from the source so that equal redistribution reads as equal volume per container; the arithmetic is unchanged.

The original artefact-fit note that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it has been removed and reframed only as 'a 2D scene suffices here' within constraints, without asserting 3D is useless in general.
The original 'a static image cannot teach this / only a live tool can' framing was softened: a fixed diagram still teaches as a reference even though it cannot be manipulated.

The reteach-prerequisite links in the source assessment (unlike-denominator and line-plot prerequisites) are retained as pedagogical intent but internal prerequisite identifiers were removed as non-portable.
The efficacy of hands-on construction over other media is stated as proposed/intended, not as a verified empirical result.

probeDeeper: 'You didn't measure any pencil at 4⅝ — should that spot still be on your scale? Why?' — probes the measurement-scale (fill-the-gaps) idea versus categories
'Why did you change both fractions into eighths before adding them?' — forces the common-denominator reason into words
Counterexample: 'If one more beaker with 0 cups joined the sharing, how much would each get now?' — tests that the fair share is total ÷ count and is sensitive to the count and to a zero
'How is this line plot different from a bar chart of favourite fruits?' — checks the measurement-vs-categorical distinction on a fresh case
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: for (1) draws a number-line scale marked in eighths and stacks a mark above each measured value, leaving the positions with no data visible as gaps (not a row of bars); for (2) adds the two fractions using a common denominator (e.g. 4⅜ + 4½ = 8⅞ inches); for (3) totals ¾+½+¼+½ = 2 cups and divides by 4 to get ½ cup each (fair share). A genuine measurement scale with gaps shown, like-denominator addition, and reading 'share equally' as total ÷ count are the marks of mastery.

errorPatterns.pattern: Line-plot-as-bar-graph: treats the distinct measurement values as categories — shows only the values that occur, side by side, with no continuous scale and no gaps for unobserved values
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the line-plot prerequisite: the axis is a measurement scale like a ruler — every eighth-position exists and must be shown, even where no pencil falls, because a measurement value is not a category
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (1) the child draws the observed lengths as separate adjacent bars/columns with no evenly-spaced number-line scale, omitting the empty positions between values

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds fractions by combining numerators and denominators instead of finding a common denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach on the unlike-denominators prerequisite: re-label all the measurements in a common unit (eighths) before adding, and check the result against the scale
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (2) or (3) the child writes something like ½ + ¾ = 2/6 (or 2/4), adding tops and bottoms rather than re-expressing over eighths first

errorPatterns.pattern: Redistribute-not-as-fair-share: does not read 'share the total equally' as total ÷ count — gives a middle value, one of the amounts, or leaves the data unchanged
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront by pouring together and sharing out: combine all the liquid (the total), then share it among the four beakers; 'equally' means total ÷ count — the fair share
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task (3) the child reports ½ because it is the most common amount, or picks a beaker's value, rather than totalling to 2 cups and dividing by 4

errorPatterns.pattern: Placement/interval slip: places a mark at the wrong fractional interval or miscounts eighths, though the plot's form is right
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: have the child re-read the scale mark and count the eighths from a labelled point; the understanding of the plot is intact, only the placement slipped
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The line plot is structurally correct but a mark sits at ⅜ where the value is ½, or an eighth is read as a quarter

responseLevels.gap: Builds a bar-graph-like display (observed values as adjacent categories, no measurement scale or gaps); adds the fractions by combining numerators and denominators; treats 'share equally' as choosing a value
responseLevels.full: Constructs a proper line plot on a fractional measurement scale with gaps shown, totals and differences measurements using common denominators, solves the equal-redistribution problem as total ÷ count (the fair share), and transfers the same reasoning to a fresh measurement set
responseLevels.partial: Constructs a correct line plot on a measurement scale and reads it, and adds fractions with like denominators, but stumbles when denominators differ or does not connect 'redistribute equally' to total ÷ count — displays and reads the data but cannot fully operate on it

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a set of measurements to the nearest 1/8 (e.g. eight pencils: 4½, 4¾, 4½, 5, 4⅜, 4¾, 4½, 5 inches) and set these tasks, WATCHING how they work. (1) 'Make a line plot to show these lengths.' (2) 'What is the combined length of the two shortest pencils?' (3) 'Four beakers hold ¾, ½, ¼ and ½ of a cup. If all the liquid were shared equally between the four beakers, how much would each hold?' (Set the task and WATCH — do not tell them to use a common denominator or hint that sharing equally is total ÷ count.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Task (1) exposes whether the child treats the axis as a measurement scale (gaps present, evenly spaced) or as bar-graph categories (only observed values, side by side). Task (3) cannot be solved by reading the plot — it requires totalling unlike fractions and dividing by the count, so it separates a child who can operate on the data from one who can only display it, and previews the mean. The two together distinguish display-only competence from full fraction-operation competence.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Pie charts
topic.description: Interpret and construct pie charts: calculate sector angles from data, draw sectors accurately, and read values from pie charts to solve problems
evidence: Read a pie chart and determine what fraction or percentage of the total each sector represents
Construct a pie chart from given data by calculating sector angles
Use a pie chart to determine the actual quantity represented by each sector given the total
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a pie chart — for example, one showing how a family spends its weekly budget — and use it to answer questions and solve problems?

pedagogy.summary: Interpret and construct pie charts as proportions of one whole. Convert each category count to its fraction of the total and then to a sector angle: (frequency ÷ total) × 360°. Recover a count from an angle only when the total is known. Move between the table, fraction/percentage, sector angle and constructed circle; check calculations and drawing rather than relying only on whether the sectors total 360°.
bestPractices: Establish the pie chart as parts of ONE whole: the full circle (360°) is the whole data set, and each sector is that category's fraction of it — so a sector shows a proportion, never a raw count

Teach sector angles as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, and always check both that the sectors sum to 360° and that each sector matches its table fraction; explicitly contrast with the wrong 'divide 360 by the frequency' and 'multiply frequency by the total' methods
To read an actual quantity from a pie chart, combine the sector (its angle/fraction) with the KNOWN total — make explicit that the raw frequency is not shown on the chart itself
Connect pie-chart angles to percentages and to the angles-at-a-point fact (360°), so children draw on proportion and angle knowledge together
Move fluently in both directions — table → angles → chart to construct, and chart + total → quantities to interpret — so the representation and the data stay linked
keyRepresentations: A circle as the whole (360°) partitioned into sectors, each labelled with its fraction/percentage of the total
The formula (frequency ÷ total) × 360° shown alongside a data table being turned into sectors
A protractor laying off each sector angle from a starting radius (the construction act)
A double representation — same data as a table and as a pie chart — to move between proportion and count
commonMisconceptions: Reading a pie sector as a raw quantity rather than a proportion of the whole — or trying to read an actual count off the chart without using the total
Calculating a sector angle by dividing 360° by the frequency (instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°)
Calculating a sector angle by multiplying the frequency by the total frequency
Not checking that the sector angles sum to 360°

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, interpret and construct pie charts. The full 360° circle is one data set; each sector angle is the category fraction of the total multiplied by 360°. Recover a count by multiplying the sector fraction by the known total. Compute the angles, draw them with a protractor, label categories, and verify each against the table as well as checking their sum. This topic does not assess line-graph mastery, which belongs to the separate Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp).

activities.title: Live pie-chart builder from class data
feedback: If the sectors do not exactly fill the circle (leaving a gap or overlapping), at least one angle is wrong — check the method and the arithmetic: each angle should be the category's fraction of the whole, taken of 360°

360 ÷ 12 = 30° (with 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) makes the sectors total only 150° — less than half the circle — so the circle itself shows the angle must be a fraction of 360°, not 360 divided by the count
After computing, total the sector angles: if they do not make 360°, find the error before drawing
The 'show actual numbers' toggle needs the total because a sector shows only a proportion — an unlabelled sector does not show the raw count on its own
activities.rationale: Construction forces the proportional idea into the open: a live repartitioning circle links the computed angle to a visible share and lets wrong methods fall visibly short of the whole circle, while the protractor step performs the actual construction act. The greyed-out count toggle makes 'sector = proportion, not count' explicit.
sourceClaims: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°

In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Enter a class data table into a tool that repartitions a circle in real time, e.g. favourite pet: dog 12, cat 6, rabbit 6, with 24 children in all
Watch dog's 12-out-of-24 sector swing open to fill exactly half the circle, with a label ticking over to 180° and 50%
Compute each sector angle yourself as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°: dog 12/24 × 360° = 180°, cat and rabbit 6/24 × 360° = 90° each
Add the sector angles and confirm they sum to 360° before drawing

Deliberately try the tempting wrong method 360 ÷ 12 = 30° for dog (and 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) and watch the sectors fall well short of closing, totalling only 150° and leaving 210° of the circle empty
Use a protractor-construction mode to lay off each computed angle from a starting radius
Use a 'show actual numbers' toggle that stays greyed out until the total is entered, making visible that a sector is a proportion, not a count
activities.intendedInsight: A pie sector's angle is the category's share of the whole circle — (frequency ÷ total) × 360° — not 360 divided by the frequency and not frequency times the total; and the sectors must sum to one whole turn, 360°.

activities.title: Recover a count from a sector and the total
feedback: Answering '90 children walk' reads the angle as a count — 90° is the angle, not the number of children
The whole circle is all 40 children; a right angle is a quarter of the circle, so a quarter of 40 = 10
Saying 'you cannot tell' misses that the total lets you recover the count — fraction of the whole × total
activities.rationale: Separating the angle/fraction from the count via the total directly confronts the sector-as-quantity misconception and makes the role of the total explicit.
sourceClaims: In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Read a given pie chart where a sector's angle is stated, e.g. 'the walk sector is a right angle, 90°, and 40 children travel in all — how many walk?'
Work out the sector's fraction of the whole: 90° is a quarter of 360°, so a quarter of 40 = 10 children walk
Try a second: 'a sector is 72° and there are 20 children altogether — how many is that?' (72/360 × 20 = 4)
State explicitly which number came from the chart (the angle/fraction) and which from the given total (the count)
activities.intendedInsight: To get an actual quantity from a pie chart you must combine the sector's fraction with the known total; the raw count is not visible on the chart itself.

activities.title: Compare same-size sectors from different totals
feedback: Equal slice sizes mean equal fractions, not equal counts — apply each chart's own total
Recover each count separately: the same fraction of different totals gives different numbers (a third of 30 = 10, a third of 12 = 4)
When a fraction of a total is not a whole number of people, re-check the data or the fraction; counts of people must be whole
activities.rationale: A counterexample with two totals tests whether the child treats a sector as a proportion rather than an absolute quantity, reinforcing the proportion-plus-total move.
sourceClaims: In a pie chart the sectors are proportional to the data; the actual frequency for each sector is usually NOT stated and must be calculated from the sector and the total — a sector shows a proportion, not a raw quantity
learnerActions: Compare two pie charts: a class of 30 and a class of 12 that both have a 'football' sector of the same size (say 120°, a third of the circle)
Decide whether the equal-size slices mean the same number of children, and justify
Work out the two actual counts using each chart's own total: a third of 30 = 10 versus a third of 12 = 4, noticing that equal fractions give different counts
activities.intendedInsight: A sector is a proportion of ITS OWN total; equal-looking sectors from different totals can represent different counts.

activities.title: Scorable checks on interpret and partial-construct skills
feedback: Choosing the '360 ÷ frequency' option usually gives sectors that do not total 360°, and even when the total happens to come out right it is not the category's fraction of the whole — the fraction-of-360 method, (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, is correct
If the fill-in count is wrong, check whether you used the total and the sector's fraction together
A correct interpretation or angle calculation is a start; construct a complete pie chart to demonstrate the drawing skill
activities.rationale: Short response formats give a scorable check of interpretation and part of construction; because choosing a correct angle is recognition rather than building, pair them with the full builder.
sourceClaims: Pie chart sector angles are calculated as (category frequency ÷ total frequency) × 360° and must sum to 360°; two named misconceptions are dividing 360° by the frequency, and multiplying the frequency by the total frequency — both corrected by taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°
learnerActions: Complete a fill-in task: 'the bus sector is 120°, there are 36 children, so ___ take the bus' (12)
Compute a sector angle from a table in a single step and enter it
Answer a multiple-choice item that includes the '360 ÷ frequency' answer as a tempting wrong option, and explain why it is wrong
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a sector with the total and computing a sector angle can be checked for accuracy; recognising a correct angle is not the same as constructing a whole chart.

assess.correctAnswer: The walk sector is 90/360 = 1/4 (25%) of the whole, so 1/4 × 60 = 15 children walk. pedagogy.summary: This is the representational craft behind correlation: plotting bivariate data as a scatter graph with correctly labelled axes and a sensible, consistent scale, describing the correlation, and drawing an estimated line of best fit BY EYE to read predictions. Three techniques carry it. First, each point represents one subject's pair of values, plotted like a coordinate — the axes must be labelled with the two variables and scaled consistently (a break in an axis is fine when values don't start near zero). Second, the line of best fit is a SINGLE straight trend line following the direction of the correlation, positioned so points are balanced roughly equally either side along its length — not a dot-to-dot join of consecutive points, and not forced through the origin. Third, the line supports INTERPOLATION (estimating within the range of the data, reasonably reliable when correlation is strong) but EXTRAPOLATION beyond the data is unreliable, because the trend may not continue. The characteristic errors are joining the dots, drawing an unbalanced line, and confidently extrapolating past the data.
bestPractices: Plot each subject as one cross using a consistent scale on both axes, labelled with the variables; use an axis break when the data doesn't start near zero rather than distorting the scale
Draw the line of best fit as ONE straight trend line in the direction of the correlation, adjusted so points are distributed as equally as possible either side along its length
Explicitly contrast a line of best fit with a dot-to-dot join — the trend line summarises the whole cloud, it does not connect consecutive points
Use the line to interpolate (estimate within the data range) and flag that estimates are more reliable when the correlation is strong
Treat extrapolation beyond the highest/lowest data values with caution — the trend is not known to continue, so such predictions are unreliable
Keep the representation tied to context so a read-off value is interpreted meaningfully (e.g. predicted score for 5 hours' revision)
keyRepresentations: A scatter of crosses on labelled, consistently-scaled axes (with an axis break where appropriate)
A single straight line of best fit through a point cloud, points balanced either side
The line of best fit contrasted with a wrong dot-to-dot zig-zag
The data range marked on the x-axis, separating the interpolation zone from the extrapolation zone

Drawing a line of best fit that is unbalanced (most points on one side) or forcing it through the origin
Extrapolating beyond the data range and treating the prediction as reliable

They use it to estimate within the data range (interpolation) while treating predictions beyond the data (extrapolation) with caution. The discriminating skill is constructing and balancing the line, and knowing where it is safe to read from.

activities.title: Plot and balance a line of best fit
feedback: If points are misplaced, check the scale is even and linear and that x- and y-values have not been swapped before re-plotting a couple of points.
To test balance, count the points above and below the line; if most are on one side, tilt or shift the line until they are roughly equal along its length.
If the learner joins the dots, contrast the zig-zag with the straight line directly: the trend line describes the general direction across all points, the join describes none.
If the line is pinned through the origin or a chosen point, note it does not have to pass through either - reposition it to balance the cloud.
activities.rationale: Plotting and balancing a line is a construction skill that is practised by doing rather than only recognising. First judge the direction of the correlation from the overall pattern (if there is no correlation, do not draw a line). Then draw a SINGLE straight trend line in that direction and adjust it (tilt and shift) until roughly equal numbers of points sit above and below along its whole length.
Deliberately draw a wrong dot-to-dot zig-zag joining consecutive points alongside the correct line, and explain in words why the single trend line, not the join, summarises the whole cloud.

activities.title: Interpolate inside, question outside

feedback: Use this as a model to compare against your own plot — does your line balance the cloud as the example does?

pedagogy.summary: At age 13-14 children meet bivariate data: they describe the RELATIONSHIP between two variables shown on a scatter graph as positive, negative or no correlation, draw a line of best fit, and use it to make predictions. Conceptually the load-bearing ideas are three. First, correlation is about a TREND across the cloud of points — the strength is how tightly the points cluster around a line, not how steep the line is. Second, and most important, correlation is NOT causation: two variables can rise and fall together because one causes the other, because a third (confounding) variable drives both, because of reverse causation, or by coincidence — so a correlation alone never proves that changing one will change the other. Third, people tend to see the correlation they EXPECT ('illusory correlation'), over-reading a relationship when they believe a causal story and under-reading one that surprises them. Teaching should ground correlation in real, meaningful pairs (temperature vs ice-cream sales), constantly ask 'what could explain this link besides cause?', and separate strength-of-correlation from steepness-of-line.
bestPractices: Ground correlation in real bivariate contexts (temperature vs ice-cream sales, revision time vs test score) and describe the TREND in words before naming positive/negative/none
Confront correlation-vs-causation head-on with classic confounded pairs (ice-cream sales and drownings; firefighters at a fire and damage) and ask what third variable could drive both

learn.summary: For ages 13–14, this guidance teaches bivariate data on scatter graphs: describing the trend between two variables as positive, negative, or no correlation; drawing a line of best fit and using it to predict within the data range; and, most importantly, separating correlation from causation. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) correlation is a trend across a cloud of points, and strength means how tightly points cluster around a line, NOT how steep the line is; (2) correlation is not causation — co-variation can arise from direct cause, a common cause (confounder), reverse cause, or coincidence; (3) people tend to see the correlation they expect ('illusory correlation'), over-reading expected links and under-reading surprising ones. Activities ground every example in real, meaningful pairs and repeatedly ask 'what else could explain this link?' A live scatter sandbox with a confounder slider is the primary proposed mechanism; a Socratic sceptic, a scorable check, a static annotated gallery, and a predict-observe-explain task are preserved as distinct complementary approaches.

activities.title: Scatter sandbox: tighten the cloud, then toggle a confounder
feedback: If a learner stretches the cloud vertically so the line gets steeper and the spread grows in proportion, point out the read-out did not change: strength depends on how tightly points cluster around the line compared with the size of the trend, not on the gradient by itself.
When the temperature slider makes ice cream and drownings rise together, prompt: 'Neither of these causes the other — what is making both go up?' to surface the common cause (hot weather).
If a learner names a direct cause for a confounded pair, ask them to check whether a single third factor could be driving both before concluding one causes the other.
activities.rationale: Correlation is a felt property of a cloud of points and its trend. Manipulating the cloud and toggling a confounder may let a learner SEE strength-vs-steepness and common-cause directly, making the abstract ideas concrete. These are proposed interaction examples (live strength read-out, draggable points, temperature slider), not mandatory mechanisms; a static annotated image could illustrate the same labelled cases without live manipulation.

learnerActions: Drag points on a scatter graph and watch a live 'strength' read-out and a best-fit line update as you move them.

Stretch the whole cloud vertically (scale every y-value by the same factor) so the trend line gets steeper and the spread around it grows in proportion, and notice that the strength read-out stays the same; then pull the points closer to the line without changing its steepness and watch the strength increase.

Move a single 'temperature' slider and watch it simultaneously push ice-cream sales UP and beach-swimming/drownings UP, so a strong positive correlation appears between ice cream and drownings even though neither causes the other.
Turn the temperature slider back down and watch both variables fall together, showing that in this model, where temperature is built in as the common cause, the hidden variable drives both.

For fresh correlated pairs, use a 'what else could explain this?' prompt to name any plausible confounder, and decide which of four explanations seems most plausible for each pair, giving a reason: direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence.
activities.intendedInsight: Strength of correlation is how closely points hug the line, not how steep the line is; and a real, strong correlation can exist between two variables when a hidden third variable drives both — so correlation alone never proves causation.

activities.title: Argue it out with a sceptical scientist
feedback: If a learner accepts the causal claim, prompt them to look for a third variable that could drive both quantities.
If a learner denies any link ('they're unrelated'), affirm that the correlation is genuinely real and redirect them to explain WHY correlated things need not be causally connected.
Reward answers that name a specific plausible confounder and state that co-variation alone does not establish causation.
activities.rationale: Judging causal claims is fundamentally reasoning, and a Socratic partner can press a learner on WHY a correlation need not be cause and surface their own causal assumptions — including the expected causal stories that drive over-reading of a link. This discussion complements, and does not replace, work with actual scatter data: a conversation cannot by itself verify plotting a graph or reading a trend, so it should be paired with the data tool.

'Illusory correlation' (Chapman & Chapman): people hold beliefs about how two variables relate that create the impression of an empirical contingency, and they overestimate the association when they believe a causal link exists between the variables
learnerActions: Respond to a character who presents tempting causal claims drawn from correlations, e.g. 'Towns with more churches have more crime — so do churches cause crime?' or 'More firefighters are sent to bigger fires and there is more damage — so should we send fewer firefighters?'
For each claim, explain in your own words what ELSE could account for the link besides one variable causing the other, and try to name the confounding common cause (e.g. town population; fire size).
When pressed, state whether the correlation is real, and separately whether the causal claim follows from it.
activities.intendedInsight: Correlation-vs-causation is an argument you can make: a real link can be explained by a confounder, reverse cause, or coincidence, so you must give a reason rather than accept the causal story.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: the firefighters data
feedback: A written reason of 'yes, fewer firefighters → less damage' reveals reading correlation as causation: introduce the confounder (fire size) explicitly, name the four explanations — direct cause, common cause, reverse cause, coincidence — and, if the learner has misread correlation itself, revisit what 'correlation' means (a trend/co-variation, not a cause).
A 'no, because they're unrelated' answer misses that the variables ARE genuinely correlated; affirm the real link and ask for the common cause.
A full answer names the confounder (fire size / summer weather) and states that variables moving together does not by itself establish that one causes the other.
activities.rationale: Requiring the reason BEFORE the reveal makes the task diagnostic: it distinguishes a learner who read correlation as causation from one who already holds the concept. Transfer to a fresh pair checks that the reasoning generalises rather than being memorised for one example.

learnerActions: Study data in which the number of firefighters sent to a fire is strongly positively correlated with the amount of damage caused.

Before any discussion, WRITE your prediction and your REASON for this question: 'If the fire service sent FEWER firefighters to each fire, would there be less damage?' Commit to both prediction and reason first.
Then observe the lurking variable — the SIZE of the fire — which drives both the firefighters sent and the damage, and compare it against your written reason.
Finally, transfer the reasoning to a fresh pair: explain what could cause BOTH ice-cream sales and drownings to rise and fall together.
activities.intendedInsight: A correlation can be fully real yet not show the effect of one variable on the other, because a confounding variable (fire size; hot weather) drives both measured quantities — so changing one variable need not change the other in the way the correlation suggests (sending fewer firefighters would likely mean more damage, not less).

activities.title: Scorable check: type, strength, and causal claims
feedback: If a learner picks the steeper-but-more-scattered graph as 'stronger', show the two scatters again and point to how tightly the points hug the line, not the gradient.
If a learner labels a clear downward trend 'no correlation', contrast the three cases: positive (up together), negative (one up as the other down), none (no trend at all).
On the causal item, require the 'why' tier: a correct 'no' must be backed by a plausible confounder or other non-causal explanation, not by denying the link.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and comparison items give a scorable check, and a two-tier causal item can catch the causation misconception and the shallow-'no' error at the 'why' tier. A recognition check confirms discrimination but does not by itself elicit the independent construction of an explanation, so pair it with the predict-observe-explain and discussion tasks.
